problem_statement: The paper frames portfolio optimization as choosing a subset of assets so as to maximize expected revenue while minimizing risk under a budget constraint. It focuses on a single-period, Boolean version of the problem.
problem_statement_quotes: portfolio optimization occupies a central role. It describes a set of n assets xi ∈{X}n from which a subset needs to be picked. The goal is to maximize the revenue while minimizing the risk at t future time steps.
For the sake of simplicity, we will focus on a single-time step modality of this problem with Boolean asset investment.
Let us consider then, a single time step t and a budget B, which defines the number of assets that can be selected.
classical_baseline: The paper treats classical solutions to the portfolio problem as the baseline, and also compares against standard quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) and finite-time digitized-adiabatic algorithms as the main prior quantum approaches. It also notes that quantum annealers and digital QAOA are commonly used for this constrained optimization problem.
classical_baseline_quotes: Several classical solutions have been proposed for this problem.
Both analog (quantum annealing) and digital (QAOA) algorithms are commonly used for solving this constrained optimization problem.

classical_difficulty: The paper says the single-period discrete portfolio optimization problem is NP-complete, and it emphasizes that QAOA-style circuits are relatively deep and therefore affected by hardware noise. It also says slow annealing is affected by decoherence, while fast evolution causes excitations that hurt solution quality.
classical_difficulty_quotes: Single-period discrete portfolio optimization has been shown to be NP-complete regardless of the risk [26].

QAOA is one of the hybrid classical-quantum approaches known as variational quantum algorithms (VQA), and it requires classical training to fit an ansatz or parametrized quantum circuit (PQC) composed of discrete gates.
Given its canonical form, it produces relatively deep quantum circuits that are known to be impacted by hardware noise [11].

By nature, quantum annealing is a slow process, therefore affected by decoherence, which leads to an accumulation of errors. To mitigate this issue, one might resort to rapid non-adiabatic evolution.
